questions.question: Why do real gases behave ideally at high temperatures?
questions.solution_html:
• Negligible intermolecular forces: At high temperatures, gas molecules have high
  • kinetic energy and move rapidly, overcoming the intermolecular attractions. As a result
  • these forces become insignificant, and the molecules behave as if they do not interact
  • with each other.
  • Negligible particle volume: Although gas molecules have finite volume, their rapid
  • motion at high temperatures makes the actual volume of the particles negligible
  • compared to the total volume of the container. Hence, under high-temperature
  • conditions, real gases closely follow the assumptions of the ideal gas model.

questions.question: What are primary and secondary standards in titrimetric analysis? Give an / example of each.
questions.solution_html:
• each.
  • Primary standards are substances of very high purity, definite composition, and high
  • stability. They are non-hygroscopic, do not react with air, and have relatively high molar
  • mass, which minimizes weighing errors. Because of these properties, they can be
  • weighed accurately to prepare a solution of known concentration directly. Examples
  • Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃), potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇).
  • Secondary standards are substances that are not sufficiently pure or stable to prepare
  • standard solutions by direct weighing. Their solutions may be hygroscopic, volatile, or
  • react with atmospheric gases (like CO₂), so their exact concentration must be
  • determined by titration against a primary standard. Examples: Sodium hydroxide
  • (NaOH), hydrochloric acid (HCl). Thus, primary standards are used to standardize
  • secondary standards, ensuring accuracy in titrimetric analysis.

questions.question: What is the main difference between solids, liquids, and gases?
questions.solution_html:
• In solids, particles are closely packed with strong intermolecular forces, restricting
  • them to vibrations only, giving a definite shape and volume.
  • Examples: Sodium chloride (NaCl), copper (Cu), diamond.
  • In liquids, particles are close together with moderate intermolecular forces, allowing
  • them to move past each other, so they have definite volume but no fixed shape.
  • Examples: Water (H₂O), ethanol (C₂H₅OH), benzene (C₆H₆).
  • In gases, particles are far apart with very weak or negligible intermolecular forces
  • moving freely, resulting in neither definite shape nor definite volume.
  • Examples: Oxygen (O₂), nitrogen (N₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂).
  • Short Essay Questions

questions.question: Describe the principle of Redox titration with a suitable example. ?
questions.solution_html:
• Redox titration is an analytical technique used to determine the concentration of a
  • substance based on an oxidation–reduction reaction involving the transfer of electrons.
  • In this process, a solution of known concentration, called the titrant, is added to a
  • solution of unknown concentration, called the analyte, until the reaction reaches
  • completion.
  • The principle of redox titration is based on the transfer of electrons between the
  • oxidizing agent and the reducing agent. Oxidation involves the loss of electrons
  • whereas reduction involves the gain of electrons. The equivalence point is reached
  • when the number of electrons lost by one species is equal to the number of electrons
  • gained by the other. The end point is usually detected by a colour change, either by
  • using suitable indicators such as methylene blue or diphenylamine, or by the self
  • indicating property of certain titrants like potassium permanganate (KMnO₄).
  • Example: In the titration of ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄) with potassium permanganate
  • (KMnO₄) in acidic medium, Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺ and MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺.
  • KMnO₄ acts as a self-indicator; the end point is indicated by the appearance of a
  • permanent light pink colour.

  • polar molecules. These molecules possess a permanent dipole moment due to an

  • In a polar molecule, one end becomes partially positive (δ⁺) and the other partially

  • Molecules with larger electronegativity differences show stronger interactions
  • Distance between molecules

  • Molecular orientation
  • Proper alignment (positive end near negative end) maximizes attraction
  • Molecular size and shape
  • Larger molecules may have stronger overall intermolecular forces, but
  • orientation effects still matter

  • Hydrogen chloride (HCl)

questions.question: Why do real gases behave ideally at high temperatures?
questions.solution_html:
• Negligible intermolecular forces: At high temperatures, gas molecules have high
  • kinetic energy and move rapidly, overcoming the intermolecular attractions. As a result
  • these forces become insignificant, and the molecules behave as if they do not interact
  • with each other.
  • Negligible particle volume: Although gas molecules have finite volume, their rapid
  • motion at high temperatures makes the actual volume of the particles negligible
  • compared to the total volume of the container. Hence, under high-temperature
  • conditions, real gases closely follow the assumptions of the ideal gas model.

  • stability. They are non-hygroscopic, do not react with air, and have relatively high molar
  • mass, which minimizes weighing errors. Because of these properties, they can be
  • weighed accurately to prepare a solution of known concentration directly. Examples
  • Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃), potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇).
  • Secondary standards are substances that are not sufficiently pure or stable to prepare
  • standard solutions by direct weighing. Their solutions may be hygroscopic, volatile, or
  • react with atmospheric gases (like CO₂), so their exact concentration must be
  • determined by titration against a primary standard. Examples: Sodium hydroxide
  • (NaOH), hydrochloric acid (HCl). Thus, primary standards are used to standardize
  • secondary standards, ensuring accuracy in titrimetric analysis.

questions.question: Explain anti-Markovnikov addition with a suitable example.
questions.solution_html:
• Anti-Markovnikov (peroxide effect or Kharasch effect) is a type of addition reaction
  • in which the substituent (such as HBr) adds to an unsymmetrical alkene in the opposite
  • manner to Markovnikov’s rule. Here, the hydrogen atom attaches to the carbon with
  • fewer hydrogen atoms, while the halide (Br) attaches to the carbon with more hydrogen
  • atoms. This occurs in the presence of peroxides via a free radical mechanism.
  • Example: Addition of HBr to propene in the presence of peroxide
  • CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CH₂–CH₂Br (1-bromopropane)

questions.question: What is the main difference between solids, liquids, and gases?
questions.solution_html:
• In solids, particles are closely packed with strong intermolecular forces, restricting
  • them to vibrations only, giving a definite shape and volume.
  • Examples: Sodium chloride (NaCl), copper (Cu), diamond.
  • In liquids, particles are close together with moderate intermolecular forces, allowing
  • them to move past each other, so they have definite volume but no fixed shape.
  • Examples: Water (H₂O), ethanol (C₂H₅OH), benzene (C₆H₆).
  • In gases, particles are far apart with very weak or negligible intermolecular forces
  • moving freely, resulting in neither definite shape nor definite volume.
  • Examples: Oxygen (O₂), nitrogen (N₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂).

questions.question: Describe the principle of Redox titration with a suitable example. ?
questions.solution_html:
• Redox titration is an analytical technique used to determine the concentration of a
  • substance based on an oxidation–reduction reaction involving the transfer of electrons.
  • In this process, a solution of known concentration, called the titrant, is added to a
  • solution of unknown concentration, called the analyte, until the reaction reaches
  • completion.
  • The principle of redox titration is based on the transfer of electrons between the
  • oxidizing agent and the reducing agent. Oxidation involves the loss of electrons
  • whereas reduction involves the gain of electrons. The equivalence point is reached
  • when the number of electrons lost by one species is equal to the number of electrons
  • gained by the other. The end point is usually detected by a colour change, either by
  • using suitable indicators such as methylene blue or diphenylamine, or by the self
  • indicating property of certain titrants like potassium permanganate (KMnO₄).
  • Example: In the titration of ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄) with potassium permanganate
  • (KMnO₄) in acidic medium, Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺ and MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺.
  • KMnO₄ acts as a self-indicator; the end point is indicated by the appearance of a
  • permanent light pink colour.

questions.question: Describe the role of hydrogen bonding in determining the boiling and / . How do intermolecular hydrogen bonds contribute CO4] to the unique physical properties of water?
questions.solution_html:
• of water. How do intermolecular hydrogen bonds contribute to the unique physical
  • properties of water?
  • Water is a polar molecule in which the oxygen atom is more electronegative than
  • hydrogen, resulting in partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charges
  • on hydrogen atoms. This polarity enables the formation of intermolecular hydrogen
  • bonds between water molecules. Each water molecule can form four hydrogen bonds
  • two through its hydrogen atoms and two through the lone pairs of electrons on oxygen.
  • This leads to the formation of a three-dimensional tetrahedral network.
  • Boiling Point of Water In water, molecules are held together by strong intermolecular
  • hydrogen bonds. To convert liquid water into steam, these hydrogen bonds must be
  • broken. Since hydrogen bonds are relatively strong, a large amount of energy (heat) is
  • required to overcome them. Therefore, water has an unusually high boiling point
  • (100°C) compared to similar molecules like H₂S, which do not form hydrogen bonds.
  • Melting Point of Water In ice, water molecules are arranged in a rigid three
  • dimensional hydrogen-bonded network. To melt ice, this structured arrangement must
  • be partially broken. This requires significant energy to disrupt hydrogen bonds
  • resulting in a relatively high melting point (0°C).
  • Properties of water due to strong intermolecular attraction between water molecules
  • (hydrogen bonding) give it exceptional thermal stability, surface properties, and solvent
  • ability, making it vital for biological and environmental systems.
  • High specific heat capacity
  • Water can absorb a large amount of heat without a significant rise in
  • temperature because energy is used to break hydrogen bonds.
  • High heat of vaporization
  • A large amount of energy is required to convert water from liquid to vapour
  • due to the need to break intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
  • High surface tension
  • Strong hydrogen bonding creates high cohesion between molecules, forming a
  • tight surface layer.
  • Density anomaly (ice floats on water)
  • In ice, hydrogen bonds form an open 3D structure, making it less dense than
  • liquid water.
  • Strong cohesion and adhesion
  • Cohesion keeps water molecules together, while adhesion allows them to stick
  • to other surfaces, aiding capillary action.
  • Excellent solvent properties
  • Due to polarity and hydrogen bonding, water dissolves many ionic and polar
  • substances effectively.

  • Point Explanation – (3 marks); Any four Unique Physical Properties – (2 marks))

questions.question: Explain the concept of dipole-dipole interactions. How do these forces arise, / ? Provide examples of substances CO4] where dipole-dipole interactions occur.
questions.solution_html:
• factors influence their strength? Provide examples of substances where dipole-dipole
  • interactions occur.
  • Dipole–dipole interactions are intermolecular forces of attraction that occur between
  • polar molecules. These molecules possess a permanent dipole moment due to an
  • unequal distribution of electrons between atoms with different electronegativities.
  • How these forces arise
  • In a polar molecule, one end becomes partially positive (δ⁺) and the other partially
  • negative (δ⁻). When such molecules come close
  • The δ⁺ end of one molecule is attracted to the δ⁻ end of another molecule
  • This electrostatic attraction forms a dipole–dipole interaction
  • For example
  • In HCl, hydrogen carries a slight positive charge and chlorine carries a slight negative
  • charge. Neighbouring HCl molecules align such that opposite charges attract.
  • Factors influencing their strength
  • Magnitude of dipole moment
  • Greater polarity → stronger dipole–dipole attraction
  • Molecules with larger electronegativity differences show stronger interactions
  • Distance between molecules
  • Shorter distance → stronger force (follows inverse relation with distance)
  • Molecular orientation
  • Proper alignment (positive end near negative end) maximizes attraction
  • Molecular size and shape
  • Larger molecules may have stronger overall intermolecular forces, but
  • orientation effects still matter
  • Examples of substances with dipole–dipole interactions
  • Hydrogen chloride (HCl)
  • Sulfur dioxide (SO₂)
  • Chloroform (CHCl₃)
  • Acetone ((CH₃)₂CO)

  • strength – (3 marks), examples of substances – (1 mark))
